title: Water on a lotus leaf (401–410)
hookLine: like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on a needle's point, pleasures don't cling
carry: in the water, not soaked by it

lines: THE DROPS BEAD UP AND ROLL OFF.
cards: Watch rain fall on a lotus pond and you'll see something a little magical. The drops land on the broad green leaves and don't soak in.
They bead up into bright little balls, roll around, and slide off, leaving the leaf completely dry.

Scientists have a name for it now, the lotus effect, and they've studied the leaf's tiny waxy bumps to make self-cleaning surfaces. Buddhists noticed it much earlier, and saw in it a picture of a free mind.

teach.h: THE DROPS ROLL OFF THE LEAF.
teach.b: Verse four hundred one, in Max Müller's English: "Him I call indeed a Brahmana who does not cling to pleasures, like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle." Two pictures.
The water rolls off the leaf. And a mustard seed, tiny and round, can't balance on a needle's point; it just drops. Notice what the verse doesn't say.
It doesn't say the rain never falls, or that pleasure never touches this person. The lotus lives in the pond. The rain lands.
Pleasant things arrive and are enjoyed, and they don't soak in and take hold.

teach.h: A MUSTARD SEED ON A NEEDLE'S POINT.
teach.b: A few verses later the mustard seed returns: passion, hatred, pride and scorn have dropped away like a mustard seed from a needle's point. The portrait keeps growing. The one who has put down the burden.
The one of deep wisdom who knows the right road from the wrong.

teach.h: THE ROD LAID DOWN TOWARD ALL.
teach.b: The one who has laid down the rod toward every living being, weak or strong, and neither kills nor causes killing.

teach.h: IN THE WATER, NOT SOAKED BY IT.
teach.b: Gentle among the violent, calm among the grasping. Speech true, useful and never harsh. Taking nothing that isn't given, long or short, large or small, good or bad.
On this third brahmana day you can hear the book gathering everything it has taught: harmlessness, patience, true speech, not taking, not clinging.
And the lotus, which grew from a rubbish heap back in chapter four, returns as the picture of the whole thing: in the water, not soaked by it.

how: The lotus is a familiar symbol in Buddhist art, often shown beneath the Buddha's seat; teachers use the water-on-a-lotus-leaf image for living in the world without clinging to it.

o: the lotus, whose leaf lets water roll off
a riverbank reed that bends but never breaks
a water lily that closes its petals at night

games.q: match each picture in today's verses.
p: can't stay on a needle's point
long or short, large or small

s: the verse says pleasure never touches this person
the rain lands; it just doesn't soak in and take hold.
the mustard seed image appears twice in these verses
once for pleasures, once for passion, hatred, pride and scorn dropping away.
the lotus effect is a real, studied property of the leaf
tiny waxy bumps make water bead up and roll off.

games.q: a wonderful meal is set in front of you. what does the lotus leaf verse suggest?
o: enjoy it fully, then let it roll off, without chasing more.
eat it all, and plan the next one.
games.why: the lotus sits in the pond and the rain lands on it; the verse honors the one who doesn't cling, not the one who never tastes.

practice: Picture a broad green lotus leaf on still water, and let a pleasant memory from today land on it like a drop of rain: a taste, a warm moment, a compliment.
Enjoy it for a breath, then watch it bead up and roll gently off into the pond, nothing lost, nothing clinging. If another drop comes, let it fall and roll off too, and rest as the leaf.

wordCard.voice: Paduma. The lotus: pleasures land and are enjoyed, then roll off like water on its leaf; they don't soak in and take hold.

orig.note: Pali paduma (Sanskrit padma): the lotus; verse 401's picture of non-clinging.

carryVoice: Your line: in the water, not soaked by it. Pleasure lands; it doesn't have to take hold. Until tomorrow.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
sources.q: Him I call indeed a Brahmana who does not cling to pleasures, like water on a lotus leaf, like a mustard seed on the point of a needle.
